== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / No information: Cross-sectional qualitative fieldwork (September 2021 interviews) with no longitudinal follow-up; participant refusal and non-response rates are not reported (PDF pp. 5-6).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable to statistical causal estimation (qualitative thematic synthesis), though substantive cross-model comparisons are confounded by community urbanisation and asymmetric reform rollout: only Charia had transitioned to CWSA utility management while Nator and Jawia had not yet transitioned, and the Consultative model was normative rather than empirically operating (PDF p. 10, p. 13).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate descriptive institutional specification, weak site-level legal verification: accurately references the Local Governance Act, 2016 (Act 936, Section 12), NCWSP, WSSDP, National Water Policy (Section 2.2.5), model by-laws, and CWSA's utility restructuring mandate, but provides no primary doctrinal citation for the CWSA statutory reform instrument or empirical audit of enacted district by-laws in the three study districts (PDF pp. 8-10, p. 12, p. 16).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: Relies on qualitative stakeholder perceptions from September 2021 key informant interviews and secondary policy documents without reporting interview/FGD guides, audio-recording or translation procedures, systematic field-observation checklists, or researcher reflexivity (PDF pp. 5-6, pp. 8-15).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak primary outcome measurement: System breakdowns, water quality, financial viability, and equity are captured solely through key informant perceptions and national/regional secondary figures (e.g., CWSA 2017 rural coverage and regional tariffs of GHS 5.20-8.0/m3), with no primary water quality testing, downtime logs, financial audits, or household survey metrics reported for Charia, Nator, or Jawia (PDF pp. 8-15).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern: Selective/incomplete reporting between Methods and Results. Despite claiming 320 participants (or 48 KIIs plus 8 FGDs with 48 residents), field observations across three named water systems, and questionnaire preparation, the Results present zero FGD quotes, zero community resident voices, zero questionnaire data, and no systematic comparison across Charia, Nator, and Jawia, alongside an unedited thesis artifact ('As highlighted in Chapter Seven', PDF p. 9) and blended researcher opinion (Section 3.8, PDF p. 13).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern / Can't tell: Purposive sampling of three Upper West Region districts/systems is appropriate in principle, but Section 2.3 contains an unresolved sample-size contradiction (320 total participants stated vs. 48 KIIs + 48 FGD participants = 96 itemised), omits site-by-site participant counts, and recruited FGD residents through local leaders/gatekeepers despite documenting chief/political interference in local water teams (PDF pp. 5-6, p. 11).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper explicitly states its central research question—how different water governance models (COM, Public Utility, and Consultative/Hybrid) influence the effectiveness, equity, and sustainability of rural and small-town water supply systems in Ghana—and explains the policy relevance of CWSA's ongoing utility reform.

A qualitative approach is appropriate for investigating stakeholder experiences, institutional governance dynamics, perceived accountability, and socio-political tensions surrounding rural and small-town water management models.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors justify a comparative qualitative case study design anchored in polycentric governance, institutional diversity, and participatory development across three purposively selected districts/water systems in Ghana's Upper West Region (Charia, Nator, and Jawia), although empirical symmetry is weakened because only Charia had transitioned to CWSA utility management at the time of fieldwork.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2, Section 2.1, Section 2.2 (PDF pp. 3-5); Section 3.3 (PDF p. 10)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Purposive sampling of water-sector stakeholders and residents is logical, but Section 2.3 contains a major unexplained contradiction—stating 320 total participants while itemising only 48 KIIs and 8 FGDs totalling 48 participants (96 total)—gives no breakdown across the three study districts, and recruited FGD residents via community gatekeepers and local leaders without addressing selection bias despite later noting political/chief interference in WSMTs.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.3 Data Collection Methods (PDF pp. 5-6); Section 3.5 (PDF p. 11)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: While KIIs, FGDs, document analysis, and field observations are listed, interview/FGD guides, recording/transcription and local-language translation protocols, and data saturation are not described. Moreover, Author Contributions mentions 'questionnaire preparation' absent from Methods, Page 9 contains an unedited thesis reference ('As highlighted in Chapter Seven'), and Results report only September 2021 Wa KII quotes with zero FGD or site-specific observation data.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.3 (PDF pp. 5-6); Section 3.2 (PDF p. 9); Author Contributions (PDF p. 17)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper includes no reflexivity discussion of the researchers' positionality, institutional affiliations, power relations with rural residents or CWSA officials, or potential bias when recruiting through community leaders and explicitly inserting 'the researcher's expertise and experiences' into Section 3.8.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: Section 2.5 explicitly reports institutional ethical clearance from the IRB of Simon Diedong Dombo University of Business and Integrated Development Studies, informed consent from participants, and anonymity protections (with a minor phrasing discrepancy in the p. 17 Declarations noting consent from 'relevant authorities for sampling').
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.5 Ethical Considerations (PDF p. 6); Declarations (PDF p. 17)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: Section 2.4 describes iterative open and axial coding in NVivo, independent double-coding of a subset to establish consensus, and multi-source triangulation. However, analytic transparency in Results is weak: zero FGD data or grassroots resident quotes appear, system-level findings for Charia, Nator, and Jawia are not systematically compared, prevalence claims ('most respondents preferred') lack counts, and empirical themes are blended with normative commentary and literature review.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.4 Data Analysis (PDF p. 6); Sections 3.1-5.1 (PDF pp. 6-15)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: The comparative findings on institutional arrangements, financing, regulatory structures, service quality, and user participation across COM, Utility, and Consultative models (Table 1, Figure 3, and Section 6) are clearly articulated in relation to the research question and present competing stakeholder viewpoints on both COM and Utility reforms, albeit heavily reliant on Wa KIIs rather than community-level data.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.1 Table 1 & Figure 3 (PDF pp. 6-8); Sections 3.2-3.7 (PDF pp. 8-13); Section 6 Conclusion (PDF pp. 15-16)

domain_ratings.justification: Narrative assessment: The study provides useful institutional context and policy-oriented synthesis on Ghana's shift from community ownership (COM) toward professionalised CWSA utility management in the Upper West Region, proposing District Water Development Boards (DWDBs). However, its empirical transferability is constrained by missing grassroots FGD voices, asymmetric transition status across the three study systems, and lack of primary operational or equity metrics.
domain_ratings.rating: Moderately valuable (useful institutional critique of Ghana's CWSA utility transition, but empirical depth is limited by absent FGD/community data and site-level evidence)
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1 (PDF pp. 2-3); Section 2.6 (PDF p. 6); Sections 3.9-6 (PDF pp. 13-16)

evidence_quotes.criterion: Sample size contradiction in recruitment reporting (CASP Q4 / selection_bias)
evidence_quotes.quote: The study involved 320 participants, utilising two data collection methods: Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs).

evidence_quotes.criterion: Itemised FGD sample showing 48 KII + 48 FGD = 96 rather than 320 participants (CASP Q4)
evidence_quotes.quote: Additionally, eight FGDs were conducted with a total of 48 participants, comprising community residents from diverse socio-economic backgrounds.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Gatekeeper recruitment of FGD participants (CASP Q4 / selection_bias)

Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of Simon Diedong Dombo University of Business and Integrated Development Studies.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Asymmetric utility-reform implementation across the three selected case systems (CASP Q3 / confounding)
evidence_quotes.quote: Currently, only the Charia water system has been fully integrated into CWSA utility management, with plans underway for the Nator and Jawia systems.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Kosoe, Osumanu, and Ogwu (2025) present a primary qualitative comparative case study examining Community Ownership and Management (COM), Public Utility (CWSA), and Consultative/Hybrid governance models for rural and small-town water supply in Ghana's Upper West Region (Charia, Nator, and Jawia systems). Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study has clear research aims (Q1: Yes), an appropriate qualitative framing (Q2: Yes) and comparative multi-site case design rationale (Q3: Yes), documented university IRB approval and informed consent (Q7: Yes), and an explicit thematic synthesis weighing stakeholder arguments for and against COM and CWSA utility reforms (Q9: Yes). However, substantial methodological concerns arise across four domains (1 No and 3 Can't tell items): (1) Section 2.3 exhibits a stark internal sample-size contradiction—reporting 320 participants overall while itemising 48 KIIs and 8 FGDs with 48 participants (96 total)—and relies on local leaders/gatekeepers for FGD recruitment without addressing selection bias (Q4: Can't tell); (2) data collection and reporting show major gaps, including omitted interview/translation protocols, a mention of 'questionnaire preparation' in Author Contributions with no quantitative component in the paper, an unedited thesis reference ('As highlighted in Chapter Seven', p. 9), and complete absence of FGD quotes or site-specific observation data in Results (Q5: Can't tell); (3) researcher reflexivity is absent, with researcher opinion explicitly blended into Section 3.8 (Q6: No); and (4) while NVivo coding and partial double-coding are described, analytic execution relies exclusively on September 2021 Wa key informant quotes and normative synthesis rather than disaggregated empirical evidence across Charia, Nator, and Jawia, only the first of which had actually transitioned to CWSA utility management (Q8: Can't tell).
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate concern (4 Can't tell / No items)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary qualitative comparative case study (semi-structured key informant interviews, focus group discussions, document analysis, and field observations)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research aims and policy context in Abstract (PDF p. 1) and Section 1 (PDF pp. 1-3); qualitative design, theoretical framework, purposive case selection (Charia, Nator, Jawia), KII/FGD sampling, NVivo thematic analysis, IRB ethics, and qualitative-only scope in Section 2 (PDF pp. 3-6); comparative thematic findings and Wa key informant quotes in Sections 3-5 (PDF pp. 6-15, including unedited 'Chapter Seven' reference on p. 9, Charia-only utility transition status on p. 10, and Section 1.1 numbering typo on p. 15); synthesis in Section 6 (PDF pp. 15-16); Author Contributions and Declarations on PDF p. 17.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: Section 2 (PDF pp. 3-6) explicitly defines and executes a primary qualitative research design combining Key Informant Interviews, Focus Group Discussions, policy document review, and qualitative field observation analysed via thematic coding in NVivo, and Section 2.6 (PDF p. 6) confirms 'the reliance on qualitative data' with no quantitative empirical component (ruling out MMAT and quantitative checklists). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the exact matching instrument.
